Fail below 95%, or on any mismatch the ledger did not predict (a silently wrong past).
- Stage: idea

### M-53 · Check out a past that git never recorded, and bisect through it
- Tier: extreme
- Domain: software archaeology and version control
- Lens: evolution in deep time: stratigraphy and ancestral reconstruction (reading a lineage's past out of its present body)
- What: `sampo excavate --age 6mo` is given a source tree with no `.git`, no changelog and no old releases, and digs its past out of its present body the way a geologist dates rock. Pass one is stratigraphy: an agent dates every line from intrinsic evidence (idioms that came and went, API vintages, naming drift, comment tense, TODOs, dead-code fossils, abstractions layered over older ones) into a layer model. Pass two peels the layers youngest-first in a worktree as a chain of commits, each of which must build and pass the tests the layer model says existed at that depth. The jaw-drop: handed only today's tarball, it returns a runnable version from months ago in which the features born since are gone and the old behaviour is back, so a regression can be bisected through a history nobody recorded, down to the reconstructed commit that introduced it.
- Prior art: git blame, clone genealogy (Kim et al., 2005) and commit untangling all start from recorded history. Stemmatics rebuilds lost manuscripts, and ancestral sequence reconstruction resurrects extinct proteins that work (Thornton's lab), but both need several descendants and neither yields a runnable program. M-27 imagines a repo's future and M-28 rewrites its recorded past; M-21 regrows missing code, where this regrows missing time. Nothing reconstructs a runnable ancestor from one snapshot.
- Better by: bisect and blame for code that arrived without history (vendored drops, squashed imports, acquisitions, a contractor's tarball), and a new per-repo measure, temporal recoverability: how many months of its own past a codebase still carries in its body.
- Novelty: 5
- Needs: a line-dating model scored against git blame on repos that do have history; a peel-chain builder in lanes where every step must be green; a sealed workspace with no `.git`, no cached older copies of the subject and no network; a scorer that compares a reconstruction with the true ancestor's hidden tests and text.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: Take three private repos already on this box with long histories and test suites, so no model has seen their past: Sampo (4,107 commits), jarvis (1,853) and volt (983). For each, export HEAD without `.git` into a sealed directory (separate HOME, no network, no other copy of the repo readable) and choose as the hidden target the commit 25% of the history back. Give `claude -p` 4 hours and $40 per repo to produce the target. Pass if, on at least 2 of the 3 repos, the reconstruction passes at least 70% of the target's own tests (never shown to it), fails at least 70% of the tests added after the target (the later features are really gone), and is closer to the target than HEAD is by at least 40% of HEAD's line distance. Fail if no repo reaches 50% on both test measures.
- Stage: idea

### M-54 · Fuse two forks that lived apart for months into one process that remembers both
- Tier: massive
- Domain: live state reconciliation and fork management
- Lens: symbiosis across versions: symbiogenesis (two lineages fuse into one individual, as the bacterium that became the mitochondrion did)
- What: When a fork and its upstream have both run for months, each with its own users and in-memory state, today they can be reunited only by an offline merge, a hand-written data migration and a restart. `sampo fuse A B` performs symbiogenesis instead: a lane merges the two codebases in a worktree into one body that serves both APIs, the harness reads both live heaps as the parent of both processes, and an agent reconciles the two realities. Entities that exist on both sides (the same user with two emails, one SKU at two prices, order 1042 issued by both forks) are matched by key and history, merged by the rule each fork's own code implies, and every true contradiction goes to a conflict report instead of being settled silently. The jaw-drop: two programs that were one a year ago and have lived separate lives since become one individual again in seconds, both clients keep talking without a reconnect, and each client's order 1042 still opens its own order.
- Prior art: git merges code but never running state. CRDTs (Shapiro et al., 2011) and Automerge merge state only for types designed to merge; master-data management and post-acquisition database consolidation merge data offline, by hand, with downtime; Cambria (Ink & Switch, 2020) translates between schema versions with hand-written lenses. Live updating (Kitsune, Erlang, M-39) changes one process's code; no system merges two living processes whose states disagree into one.
- Better by: forks stop being one-way. A customer-specific fork, a regional deployment or an experiment that kept running can rejoin the mainline with its users and data, and divergence becomes a reviewable list of contradictions instead of a migration project.
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: heap access to both processes from their common parent; a code merge that serves both forks' APIs; entity matching across two heaps; merge-rule inference from each fork's handlers; identifier namespacing so IDs either side handed out stay valid; the conflict report as an approval artifact; an SCM_RIGHTS handover from two processes to one.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: Before the run, fork a 400-line in-memory Python service (users, orders, inventory, counters) and land 8 different features on each fork. Run both forks as children of the experiment script, each driven by its own scripted client for 5,000 requests from fixed seeds with 30% shared users and SKUs, and plant 20 contradictions whose list is sealed (also run reference copies of each fork on the same seeds). Run the fusion with `claude -p`, capped at 3 hours and $30. Pass: no request from either client fails across the fusion; over 1,000 further requests per client, every answer about an entity only one fork held matches that fork's reference; every order ID either client holds still resolves to its own order; and the conflict report names at least 18 of the 20 planted contradictions with none of them merged silently. Fail otherwise.
- Stage: idea

### M-55 · Shrink a 100k-line program into a runnable 3k-line twin, think there, and lift the edit back
- Tier: extreme
- Domain: program abstraction and agent cognition at codebase scale
- Lens: impossible list × mind (memory, attention): an agent with no context limit because the codebase carries its own mind-sized model
- What: `sampo homunculus` distils a large program into a twin small enough for a model to hold whole: a 2–5k-line runnable Python program that keeps the essential behaviour (the public commands and the state they change) and replaces the accidental parts (caching, retries, plumbing, compatibility shims) with stubs that replay their recorded behaviour. Every node of the twin keeps an origin map to the real code it stands for, and the twin must agree with the real program on recorded inputs before anyone may work in it. The agent never opens the real repo: it plans, edits and tests in the twin, where a full test run takes milliseconds. A lift step then carries the edit down, moving hunks on mapped nodes along the origin map and turning hunks on stubbed regions into small synthesis jobs that each see one real region, with the twin's diff as their spec, until the real repo passes its gates. The jaw-drop: an agent that has never been shown a line of Sampo's 100k lines of library code lands a cross-cutting change in them, and the twin, diffed against the real code, draws a measured line between Brooks's essential and accidental complexity (where the real program disagrees with its own twin on an input, the bug is in the accidental part).
- Prior art: program slicing (Weiser, 1981) and test-case reducers (C-Reduce, 2012) shrink a program while keeping a property, but only in one direction: nobody edits the reduced program and carries the edit back. CEGAR abstraction refinement (Clarke et al., 2000) builds abstract models for checking, not for editing. Bidirectional transformations (Boomerang lenses, Foster et al., 2007) put edits back through a view, but for data and with hand-written lenses, and UML-to-code round-trip engineering is known to break. Aider's repo map, RAG and recursive language models (Zhang and Khattab, 2025) choose which real text to show; M-24 splits the repo among resident cells. None runs the agent on an executable abstraction and lifts its edits down to the real code.
- Better by: repo size stops being bounded by context, because the agent's working memory is a program the size of a mind, kept honest by agreement checks; and every repo gains a runnable essence that doubles as a second oracle for its own accidental code.
- Novelty: 5
- Needs: a twin builder (slice from the public commands, stub with recorded I/O, keep origin maps, shrink until agreement drops); an agreement gate on recorded inputs; a lift compiler (hunk transport along origin maps plus per-region synthesis lanes); a resync step that rebuilds the twin after every real commit; long-running lanes on one budget.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: Build a twin of Sampo's task-and-evidence path (`sampo task`, `sampo check` and the state they write) of at most 5k lines that agrees with the real code on at least 95% of the CLI calls recorded from its own tests. Draw 10 past cross-cutting tasks in that path with `sampo louhi long gen --from .`, each in a throwaway worktree, nothing landed. Arm A: `claude -p` on the real repo with its normal tools. Arm B: `claude -p` shown only the twin and the task (under 16k tokens in all, real-repo reads refused), then the lift step by fresh `claude -p` calls that each see one real region. Pass if arm B lands at least 7 of 10 with the tasks' own acceptance commands green on the real repo, using no more tokens than arm A. Fail if no twin under 5k lines reaches 90% agreement, or if the lift fails on more than 4 of the 10 (then edits do not flow down an abstraction).
- Stage: idea

### M-56 · Give code a second dependency graph that runs through the minds that wrote it
- Tier: extreme
- Domain: software provenance and agent cognition
- Lens: impossible list × mind (perception): software that notices it is wrong before any test, by tracking what its authors perceived
- What: Every dependency graph today runs through code; Sampo adds one that runs through minds. Its hooks already see every Read, Grep and Edit, so each hunk an agent writes is wired to the exact regions (content-hashed) its author had read before writing it. When one of those regions later changes, anywhere in the repo, Sampo replays the authoring step in a worktree with the new text spliced into the recorded session; if the author, shown today's code, would now write something different, the line is flagged with that diff, which is wrongness perceived before any test and without a spec. When a bug is fixed, Sampo replays the session that introduced it with its read regions neutralised one at a time (a name made literal, a comment dropped, an example rewritten, behaviour unchanged) and bisects to the region that made its author err, which is usually correct, fully tested code. The jaw-drop: a 12-line helper with green tests turns out to be the read-ancestor of 9 bugs in 6 other files over four months, and with one misleading parameter name renamed, replays of those 9 sessions write none of them.
- Prior art: git blame and data provenance tie lines to commits and people, never to what the author was reading. Program slicing and change-impact analysis follow code dependencies only. Linguistic antipatterns (Arnaoudova et al., 2013) and misleading-identifier studies rely on hand-written rules about names. Context attribution (ContextCite, 2024) ablates context to explain one model answer, and automated failure attribution (Who&When, 2025) asks an LLM judge which step failed. W-B4 replays a session with the user's correction injected. None keeps a repo-wide graph from lines to the regions their authors read, or proves by replay that correct code causes bugs elsewhere.
- Better by: a new defect class (correct code that misleads its readers) becomes visible and fixable at its cause, and a line can be caught going stale from a change in a file it never calls, at the commit that did it.
- Novelty: 5
- Needs: read-set capture in the PostToolUse hook (region, hash, session, turn); a store linking hunks to read-sets that survives rebases and moves; a session replayer that splices new text into a recorded transcript and re-runs one step with `claude -p` several times (the step is stochastic, so a flag is a rate, not one run); behaviour-preserving neutralisers proven by the tests; a bisection driver with a token budget.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: From Sampo's own history, take 20 FIX tasks whose bug was introduced by an earlier agent session whose transcript is still under ~/.claude/projects (its Read and Edit calls give the read-set after the fact). Replay each introducing step 8 times with `claude -p` to measure its bug rate, then bisect over its read regions with behaviour-preserving neutralisers, 8 replays per probe. Pass if, for at least 8 of the 20, neutralising one region cuts the bug rate by half or more (p < 0.05 against the unneutralised replays), and at least 2 regions are the ancestor of 2 or more different bugs. Fail if fewer than 4 bugs replay at a rate of at least 3 in 8 (then replays do not reproduce authoring errors well enough to measure), or if the found regions do no better than neutralising a random read region of the same size.
- Stage: idea

### M-57 · Rewrite the codebase until every mind's blind guess about it comes true
- Tier: extreme
- Domain: API design and machine cognition
- Lens: impossible list × mind (imagination): instead of the agent learning the code, the code moves into the model's prior, so there is nothing left to read
- What: Agents spend most of their tokens reading code to learn what things are called and how they behave, and they still hallucinate; Sampo turns the hallucinations into the design authority. Blind probes give fresh `claude -p` agents a task and the repo's file list but no source, docs or `--help`, and log every call, flag, name, signature and expected result they invent, alongside the phantom calls from real sessions (an unknown `sampo` verb, an AttributeError) and users' failed attempts. Where independent guesses agree and the real code differs, a lane makes the guess true (an alias, a renamed parameter, a missing obvious helper, a default moved to what everyone expected), each change proven against the repo's tests and recorded traffic and kept only if it raises blind-guess accuracy on a held-out probe set. The code adapts to the minds that use it, not the other way round, and because every model shares much of the same prior, each change pays off for models that do not exist yet. The jaw-drop: after a few rounds, an agent that has never read the repo writes correct calls into it 9 times in 10, because the repo now is what models already believed it was.
- Prior art: "On the naturalness of software" (Hindle et al., 2012) and Ray et al. (2016) measure how predictable code is to a language model and find buggy lines less natural; naming tools suggest one name at a time. Soundslice (2025) built an import feature by hand because ChatGPT kept telling users it existed, and slopsquatting attackers register the package names models hallucinate. llms.txt (2024) writes docs for models and leaves the code alone. The principle of least astonishment is advice to designers, not a measured loop. M-43 moves a codebase away from the prior into a new language, and this moves it toward the prior. No system measures models' blind guesses about a codebase and evolves the code until they come true.
- Better by: reading cost and hallucination rate fall together for every future model without training any of them, and blind-guess accuracy becomes a measured property of a codebase: how much of it a stranger already knows.
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: a blind-probe runner with call and expectation capture; harvesting of phantom calls from session transcripts and the Ward's tool results; consensus clustering across independent sessions; materialisation lanes (alias, rename with deprecation, helper, default change) with behaviour proofs; held-out probes so the code is not tuned to what it learned from; for Sampo's own CLI, every change built as a candidate in a worktree that lands only with the user's core yes.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: Write 40 small tasks that drive Sampo's CLI and library (status, capture, task, evidence and check flows), 20 for training and 20 held out. Run each training task blind 5 times with `claude -p` (no source, docs or `--help`), and add the phantom verbs and flags already in local transcripts ("invalid choice", "unrecognized arguments"). Precheck: if fewer than 30% of phantom names recur across 3 or more independent runs, there is no shared prior to converge on, so fail. Otherwise materialise the top 15 consensus phantoms as aliases or thin helpers in a throwaway worktree with Sampo's own tests green, and measure blind first-try success on the 20 held-out tasks (5 runs each) before and after. Pass if it doubles or reaches 80%, with no rise in calls that run but do the wrong thing. Fail if it rises by less than 15 points.
- Stage: idea

### M-58 · Build software that cannot lie: every message it prints is proven as it prints it
- Tier: massive
- Domain: runtime verification and program honesty
- Lens: impossible list × mind (perception, self-knowledge): software that notices it is wrong before any test, because it checks what it says against what it did
- What: Programs talk all the time ("Saved", "3 files deleted", "Payment complete", "You're up to date", "All checks passed"), and nothing ties a sentence to the state it describes. `sampo honest` reads every user-facing string in a repo (format strings, CLI output, flash and HTTP messages, log lines at info and above), compiles each into the proposition it asserts about state with its arguments bound, and has a separate lane write an independent checker that observes that state by a different path than the code that printed it (read the file back from disk, re-query the row, count what is left in the directory). The checkers are woven in at each emission site, so in shadow mode every utterance is judged true or false at the instant it is made, and in strict mode a lie becomes a crash that quotes the sentence; programs without source get the same treatment through a pty wrapper that checks recurring output claims. The jaw-drop: run over a repo's own test suite and a week of recorded use, it finds messages that had been lying all along under green tests (a "Saved" on a path where the write failed silently), and the terminal strikes through pip's "Successfully installed" when the package will not import.
- Prior art: certifying algorithms (McConnell, Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011) emit witnesses that simple checkers verify, but for textbook algorithms written by experts. Runtime verification (JavaMOP and its kin) and Daikon-style invariants check properties someone wrote or mined from traces, never the program's own words. N-version programming compares whole implementations. Sampo's `prove --docs` checks what docs say about a CLI, offline. Proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997) proves the safety of machine code. None treats every sentence a program says as a proposition and checks it at the moment it is said.
- Better by: a lie, meaning a message that misstates state, is caught on real inputs at the instant it happens, including on paths no test reaches; and honesty becomes a measured property of a program (lies per thousand utterances).
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: a harvester for emission sites and their format arguments; a proposition compiler (sentence to typed claim over state); a checker lane barred from importing the emitting code path; an AST weaver for Python and a pty wrapper for programs without source; shadow and strict modes; a lie ledger; a cap on checker cost per utterance.
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: In a throwaway worktree of Sampo, harvest every user-facing message that asserts a state change or a count, compile and weave checkers for the first 100, and run the full test suite, `sampo drill` (its fault-planted scripted day) and `sampo demo` in shadow mode. Separately plant 10 lies by mutating emitting paths (a write that silently fails, an off-by-one count) without touching the messages. Pass if the checkers catch at least 8 of the 10 planted lies, raise false alarms on fewer than 1% of utterances and add under 20% to the suite's runtime; report any real lie found in the unmutated runs. Fail if they catch fewer than 6, or if more than 10% of the 100 messages cannot be compiled into a checkable proposition at all (then most messages are not claims about state).
- Stage: idea

### M-59 · Fuse two small models into a lichen that outthinks the frontier model neither can match
- Tier: xhigh
- Domain: model orchestration and small-model uplift
- Lens: ecology: symbiosis (a lichen is an alga and a fungus that become one organism neither can be alone); crossbred from "Pair two weak models as a lichen" × "Rate each local model as a symbiont, with a cheater cut-off"
- What: Sampo pairs a fast small model (the alga: a 4B that proposes) with the large local model (the fungus: the 27B that holds structure and memory) and evolves the exchange between them over nightly rounds on Sampo's own closed tasks: what each passes the other, when, and in what shape. Neither model is fine-tuned. The protocol is the organism, kept as a versioned card the pair carries. The jaw-drop is a pair that closes held-out tasks the frontier model closes, at no cloud cost, while each partner alone closes half as many.
- Prior art: mixture-of-agents and LLM debate (fixed protocols, peer models); speculative decoding (a small model drafts tokens for a large one, by a hand-fixed protocol); Sampo's routing (local first, then Haiku, never a pair).
- Better by: the protocol is evolved and selected on the user's own held-out work, and the pair is judged against the frontier arm, not against either partner.
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: T-2878 (a Louhi smith arm on local models), T-2917 (small-model playbooks kept on lift)
- Unblocks: none
- Kill: on 20 train-split Louhi scenarios, run the 4B alone, the 27B alone and three hand-written pair protocols (propose and critique, outline and fill, test-first and implement), graded by each scenario's hidden checks. Viable if the best pair beats the better partner alone by 5 or more scenarios; not-yet if by 1 or fewer.
- Stage: idea

### M-60 · Grow a mycorrhizal network under every repo on the machine, trading failure shapes as nutrients
- Tier: massive
- Domain: cross-project learning
- Lens: ecology: mycorrhizal networks (fungi join the roots of different trees and carry carbon and alarm signals between them); crossbred from "Grow a mycorrhizal lesson network between repos and lanes" × "Federate failure shapes between Sampo installs"
- What: Every repo Sampo serves grows hyphae: compressed failure shapes from its proven fixes, the outline of a bug's syntax and data flow and never its code. The network carries each shape to repos whose code is near it, and a repo that receives one is warned before it writes that bug. Trees that fix more feed more. A sensitive repo neither sends nor receives. Over months the network learns which of the user's repos are kin, and a new repo is inoculated from its nearest kin on day one.
- Prior art: GitHub's multi-repository variant analysis (people write the query for one known bug); Semgrep registry rules (shared by hand); federated learning (shares gradients, not failure shapes); Sampo's lessons (one project's).
- Better by: shapes move by measured kinship between the user's own repos, unasked, and a delivered warning counts only when the receiving repo later fixes that shape.
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: a failure-shape miner from proven FIX tasks (the miner M-22 also needs), kinship from import graphs and stack cards, a cross-project store under the sensitive rule
- Unblocks: M-22
- Kill: over every project in Sampo's state with 5 or more proven FIX tasks, ask of each fix whether a shape mined from another project's earlier fixes flags the lines the fix changed, before the fix, at under one false flag per 2,000 lines. Report each project's era (first and last fix date) and fail the run if the eras don't overlap. Viable if 10% or more of fixes were foreseen by a kin repo; not-yet if under 3%.
- Stage: idea

### M-61 · Breed a Red Queen: a predator that evolves new bugs against Sampo's own detectors every night
- Tier: massive
- Domain: verification by adversarial co-evolution
- Lens: ecology: Red Queen dynamics (predator and prey must keep evolving to stay where they are); crossbred from "Run a Red Queen arms race between generator and critic" × "Reintroduce an apex predator into the funnel"
- What: A predator lineage on the local models writes plausible bugs into throwaway copies of the user's repos, aimed at slipping past Sampo's finders, guard, review lenses and tests. Every bug that escapes is a lesson the prey (the detectors) must learn before the next night, and every detector that improves forces the predator to evolve. Both populations are scored, and the arms race's trace is a living map of where Sampo is blind.
- Prior art: mutation testing (random, not adaptive); coverage-guided fuzzing (finds crashes, not quiet logic bugs); GANs (images, not code); LLM red-teaming (prompts); Sampo's hunk-mutation proof (T-0271), which mutates one task's hunks once.
- Better by: the bug writer adapts to the detectors Sampo actually runs, and the detectors are scored only on bugs nobody wrote for them, on the user's own code.
- Novelty: 4
- Needs: T-2910 (local brainstorm volume), the exam's planted-defect renderer, a night slot (T-2916)
- Unblocks: M-22
- Kill: on the exam's throwaway repos, have the local 27B write 100 bugs over three rounds, each round shown which earlier bugs `sampo find` caught. Viable if the third round's escape rate is at least twice the first's (the predator learns); not-yet if it is flat.
- Stage: idea

The novelty marks above are the author's. `fm genesis novelty` marks the obvious ones by a cold read, and a typed mark
counts for nothing.

# Mission — the exam (gen 1, #13 + #6)

Task: T-2079 (fm exam). Site: T-2080 (this tower on the site).

Scope: #13's exam (gen-0 §4) and #6 Verifying anything in the part the exam proves: a fix counts only when a
hidden check outside the repo passes, a reading only when it matches the key's readings ("does it do what the user
meant"), and a result that proves nothing is labelled (errored, smoke, provisional), never scored. #6's other proofs
(UI, data, infra and ops, the unproven rollup) are Mission 7's (mission-proof.md, seed row 7).

Self-contained for a fresh `fm run` in ~/.claude/foreman. Parent: gen-1/seed.md → gen-0.md §4.

## Charter (binds this Mission as written)
gen-0's lines, verbatim:
- MUST: full autonomy. Every decision through fm decide. Never ask me anything mid-run.
- MUST: no spend cap on building and proving. Tokens go into Foreman's code and its tests, not into sweeping the outside world. Waiting out a usage limit is fine.
- MUST: everything finishes completely. A capability is done only when it has its tests, its exam scenarios passing (§4), docs (MASTER.md, README where it belongs, CHANGELOG), a site page if it's user-facing, a pane/status surface if it has state, and it works on every surface it belongs on (Claude Code, fm code, other agents, Desktop).
- MUST: unprompted actions stay local and reversible (a lane, a branch, a spike, a throwaway folder). Anything that leaves the machine needs its grant, so it goes into the final report.
- NEVER: clone or sweep outside repos to brainstorm or to benchmark. Outside material is only allowed in the targeted form in §5.
- NEVER: grant yourself anything or lower your own guard. Protected core gets a built, evaluated candidate in a worktree plus `fm ask ID core` at the end. Merging Foreman changes stays my call.

Standing intent (plugin/templates/standing-intent.md), verbatim:
A harness that figures out and does everything itself. The user's only jobs are gen-0's goals and a yes to what leaves the machine or touches protected core. Every steer is a miss to learn from.

1. Anticipate: generalize the pattern behind each steer; before filing a tower doc, ask what the user would say if they read it now, and act on that first; more ambitious, complete, general and honest, with less hand-holding.
2. Act, don't advise: a capability counts only when real sessions use it by default; one a session doesn't call is a top gap.
3. Next-level, not polish: tier 3-4 first, one moonshot a generation, nothing killed for ambition; a failure goes to not-yet and is retried.
4. Complete, and the frame grows: a capability is done with its tests, exam, docs and every surface; new capabilities, rows, lenses and exam kinds are added with evidence.
5. General: ecosystem tools, structure-aware parsing and runtime signals over hand-written rules.
6. Truth over self-image: signals Foreman didn't author; a check that measures format instead of substance is a bug.
7. Spend where it decides something.
8. Every lesson becomes code: a rule plus an automatic check, in the same task.
9. Never trade safety for autonomy.

## Capability (gen-0 §4)
Locally generated throwaway repos in at least 6 languages with planted defects (bugs, vulns, missing tests, slow
paths, docs drift, a flaky test, a broken dep) plus vague goals, ambiguous requests, a task needing a missing tool and
"no request" scenarios, all with hidden answer keys. One third held out for grading only. Scores to
research/genesis/exam.jsonl: found vs key, false alarms, readings/approaches vs key, failing-test-first fixes, tokens
per verified result.

## Gaps this Mission targets (gap-map #13, cross-cutting "No exam exists"; tooling built in T-2079; each gap stays open until a scored, child-authored held-out run in the end-of-run exam shows it closed)
- Multi-language exam generator with hidden keys and holdout — tier 3.
- exam.jsonl scoring that every later Mission, critique and selection reads (found, false alarms and hidden-check
  fixes; tf-first counts toward closing a scenario) — tier 3.
- A free, deterministic agent arm (Foreman's own finders) so every task can re-run the exam without paid sessions — tier 3.
  It costs nothing; it doesn't score well (it finds and never fixes: 0 fixes on s0-001 and s7-004), and the exam says so.

## Toolchains here
python3, node 26 (runs .ts by type stripping), cargo/rustc, ruby (no minitest: plain asserts), gcc, bun. No javac,
no go. Six runnable languages: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Ruby, C, each re-proven per run by the exam of
the exam's check 1 (`fm exam check RUN` builds every rendered repo and runs its hidden checks; test_exam renders all six).

## Approaches
A. **Chosen** — one small app API described once (functions + cases), rendered per language; each defect kind is a
   variant of one function body or file; a seeded generator picks language × defects × names, writes the repo, keeps
   the key and the hidden checks outside it. Varied by seed, so no single scenario's text can be memorised, but the template set
   itself is learnable, which is why C's outside author writes the scored held-out third; keys are true by construction.
B. Hand-written fixture repos in bench/: fixed, memorisable, the held-out third leaks the moment anyone reads it.
C. **Also chosen (standing rule 5)** — a separate tool-less child (`fm exam gen --author child`) writes whole scenarios
   from the scenario format alone, never Foreman's code or the Missions; the harness keeps only those that pass the
   exam of the exam below. Outside-authored, so its held-out scores rank gaps; A stays the free fixture and reference
   author (`--author self`), and each result records its author.
D. Plant into the project's own code (fmbench's planted-bug): one language, no request-shape scenarios. Kept as is.

## Design
- `fm exam gen [--seed N] [--per-kind 9] [--lang L,..] [--kind K,..] [--split train|holdout|all] [--author self|child]` (default self: free and deterministic, the fixture the zero-token arms and
  tests run on, never a ranking score; a run that ranks gaps passes `--author child`, each result records its author,
  and a held-out kind the child can't author yet ranks nothing until it can; standing rule 5) (child: the tool-less outside author of C, which never sees Foreman's code or the Missions; self: the template reference) → `<p.dir>/exam/<run>/<scenario>/repo` (a git
  repo, one commit) and `.../key.json` + `.../hidden/` (outside the repo). With the 11 kinds above that is 99 scenarios, 33 held out (s0-001 is that run; its 108 keyed defects, 36 in the
  held-out third, count defects, not scenarios). Split by stable hash of the scenario id; per kind, candidates are drawn until each split's quota is full: held out = (n+2)//3 (9 → 3), train = the rest, so every capability exam has ≥ 9 scenarios and ≥ 3 held out.
- Scenario kinds: bug, vuln, untested, slow, docs, flaky, dep (one planted defect, request names the area or none),
  vague ("make this faster"/"make this great": key lists readings and approach keywords), ambiguous (two readings
  the key names both of), missing-tool (key: a capability miss recorded, no false done), none (3–4 defects, no request).
- Every scenario's key.json carries its own commands (suite build/run, each hidden check's file and command), so the
  grader reads only key.json + hidden/ and a child-authored scenario grades the same as a template one.
- `fm exam run RUN --agent oracle|empty|finders|foreman|plain [--split …]`: oracle/empty calibrate; finders =
  Foreman's deterministic finders, no session; foreman = one headless session per scenario with the plugin; plain =
  the same session without it (the head-to-head of rule 5, same held-out scenarios), each with its cost
  recorded beside its score (fmbench._session). foreman and plain are paid: they run in the end-of-run exam and for a
  regressing capability only (steer 1). `--budget` no longer defaults to $2 a session (T-2179: a
  dollar cap on proving is what gen-0's "no spend cap on building and proving" rules out); the timeout stays as the
  runaway stop.
- `fm exam grade RUN`: per scenario, findings (captured tasks in the scenario's Foreman state + the reply) matched to
  the key by file + symbol; false alarms; hidden checks run for fixes; a fix counts as failing-test-first when the
  agent's suite passes on its fix and fails with the planted file put back; the planted and clean files differ only at
  the defect, so a red there is the defect caught (limit, open: an arm that also changed other code in that file can
  go red for that and be credited; T-2203 puts back only the defect's lines and credits nothing when they no longer
  apply). Appends one line per run to research/genesis/exam.jsonl
  (split, agent, found/keyed, false alarms, readings hit, fixes, tf-first, cost, tokens per verified result).
- `fm exam` (status): last runs and scores, train vs holdout.
- `fm exam scorecard`: one row per capability from held-out, non-smoke lines; a capability whose free arm beats its
  session arm prints first as `top gap:` (steer 3, `fmgenesis.free_beats`). Open (T-2204): it counts template
  (`self`) held-out scenarios too, which the Design above says never rank; until T-2204 lands its rates are provisional. The next seed opens with the same check
  on train lines as `Top gap:` (T-2184): held-out lines only grade, so no seed ever reads them.
- Session paths: the Genesis line every session starts with names the next step (fmgenesis.step). Once a
  generation's Missions and critiques are in, that step is `fm genesis select N`, which refuses without a graded line
  and names `fm exam run RUN --agent A`, then `fm exam grade RUN --agent A`; `fm genesis check` and sweep's exam row
  say the same. So a session reaches the exam by following its next step: per generation the zero-token arms (steer 1), and the
  paid arms only in the end-of-run exam.

## Exam of the exam (its own held-out checks)
1. Every generated repo builds and its visible tests pass (the defect is hidden, not a broken build) — except flaky
   (passes most runs) and dep (fails to import by design).
2. Every hidden check fails on the planted repo and passes on the clean render of the same scenario.
3. A perfect oracle agent (the key itself as findings, the clean render as the fix) scores 100% found, 0 false alarms,
   and every fix passes its hidden check; an empty agent scores 0 found. tf-first isn't part of this calibration:
   it judges the arm's own tests, which an oracle doesn't write, so it's reported, never calibrated on.
4. Holdout ids never appear in a `--split train` generation.

## Done when
`fm exam gen/run/grade` work in all six languages; the four checks above are tests; the finders arm's baseline score
is in exam.jsonl; MASTER.md + CHANGELOG + site catalogue line; README names `fm exam` beside Genesis; MCP `exam_scorecard` and the Genesis line show it (T-2172; seen live 2026-10-30: session start printed "Genesis: gen 1 · exam 0/13 pass, 4 Haiku skipped");
`fm genesis` status shows the latest exam score; the end-of-run exam's session arms are scored with none cut off by a dollar cap (T-2179 removed the default cap; open until that exam runs).

```
FEATURE: fm exam — multi-language generated exam with hidden keys, holdout third, finders + claude arms, exam.jsonl scores
DONE-WHEN: generated repos build and hidden checks fail-planted/pass-clean in python, js, ts, rust, ruby, c
DONE-WHEN: an oracle agent scores 100% and an empty agent 0%; holdout never leaks into --split train
DONE-WHEN: every surface it belongs on shows the numbers `fm exam scorecard --json` computes from exam.jsonl (passing capabilities, smoke lines skipped): the CLI, the site's Genesis page (section D, from `fm genesis export`), MCP `exam_scorecard` for Desktop and other agents, the pane and fm code's status (the Genesis line, T-2172); a test seeds exam.jsonl and compares each surface's numbers to the scorecard's, not just that a line appears
DONE-WHEN: the end-of-run exam's exam.jsonl lines show every production-model session arm on a held-out scenario scored, none errored by a dollar cutoff, judged on those lines, not on a unit test
DONE-WHEN: #13's `fm genesis exam` fails a drafted gen-0 missing any whole standing-intent clause (steer 7; T-2191, test_genesis), and every steer's rule carries its automatic check (`fm decide --check`)
DONE-WHEN: `fm exam scorecard` prints first a capability whose free arm beats its session arm on held-out lines, and the next seed opens with the same check run on train lines, since held-out lines only grade (steer 3)
DONE-WHEN: a test follows fmgenesis.step past a generation's Missions to `fm genesis select N` and gets a refusal naming `fm exam run` and `fm exam grade`, so a session reaches the exam by its next step
DONE-WHEN: test-first credit comes only from the defect's own lines put back, never from an arm's other edits in that file (T-2203)
DONE-WHEN: the scorecard ranks only child-authored held-out scenarios, never template ones (T-2204)
DONE-WHEN: each exam.jsonl line reports recall per language and per defect kind (steer 4; T-2185), so a blind spot in one language can't hide in the total
DONE-WHEN: the end-of-run exam's scored held-out third is child-authored (`fm exam gen --author child`) for every kind in `fmexam.CHILD_KINDS`; a kind the child can't author yet ranks nothing until it can (its template scenarios are labelled `self` and never ranked)
```

The DONE-WHEN lines are this Mission's finish line, not claims that it is met.

Status 2026-10-30, by DONE-WHEN line above. "Built" means code plus a unit test, named; none is exam-proven until the
end-of-run exam (steer 1). Lines 1-2 are about the exam's own soundness, not any arm's score (arms' scores, such as
s0-001's 13 false alarms, are what the exam reports):
1. built: `fm exam check` on s0-001; test_exam renders all six languages.
2. built: test_exam (oracle 100% found, empty 0; a train generation never holds a holdout id).
3. open: each surface shows the line; no test yet compares its numbers to the scorecard's (test_genesis checks the
   line's shape, test_mcp only a capability name).
4. open: needs the end-of-run exam.
5. built, and only a presence check: test_genesis drops each whole clause and expects `_misses` to fail the draft.
   A draft that repeats the clauses and ignores them still passes it; whether a generation acts on them is judged by
   drift and the critiques, and by the end-of-run exam. Each steer rule names its check with `fm decide --check`.
6. built: test_genesis (`top gap:` on held-out lines, `Top gap:` in the seed from train lines).
7. open: select's refusal names both verbs in code (fmgenesis.select), untested.
8. open: T-2203.  9. open: T-2204.  10. open: T-2185.  11. open: needs the end-of-run exam's child-authored run.

Spend (standing intent 7, steer 1): each generation runs only the zero-token arms (oracle, empty, finders) plus at
most one Haiku smoke run on 9 or fewer held-out scenarios, which never decides; production-model session arms run in
the end-of-run exam and for a capability that regresses. Every result records its cost beside its score (cost and
tokens per verified result in exam.jsonl). Deferring the paid head-to-head is the user's steer 1, so until the end-of-run
exam every selection is provisional and lineage.md says so. Foreman sets no cap on proving (gen-0); a budget the user sets with
`fm budget` is the user's own.

Task: T-2135, T-2136, T-2137, T-2138, T-2139, T-2140, T-2141 (briefs 1–7 in order). T-2135 is L: today's spent risk budget is Foreman's own guard, which
gen-0 forbids lowering, and it holds L self-approval until it resets on 2026-10-31; no question goes to the user,
and then the plan takes the normal L path under full autonomy (a self-critique, then `fm decide`). Nothing is
granted around the guard while it's spent; the run waits it out, as it would a usage limit.

Self-contained for a fresh `fm run` in ~/.claude/foreman. Parent: gen-1/seed.md → gen-0.md §2 #4, §3.
Ideas: 308 from `fm ideas --rounds 4 --falsify --crossbreed --seen` (mission pack research/mission-20261030-053122.md;
`--deepen` didn't run: the spent risk budget drops optional rounds, a guard Foreman never lowers itself; decisions.md
2026-10-30 "Mission 4 brainstorm ran without --deepen", revisit after 2026-10-31: the deepen rounds rerun and merge
here), lenses below; placed by tier
after merging duplicates.

## Capability (gen-0 §2 #4)
Turn a vague goal into a complete plan: what a finished, best-in-class version contains, decomposed and ordered. It
carries the plan over days, across crashes and compactions, and knows when it's actually done rather than merely
stopped.

## What the last Missions taught
- Precision over volume (Mission 2, 3): both session arms found every planted defect and closed no scenario. For #4
  the same trap is "done": a session that says done while a contents item is missing is the false alarm here.
- A live arm finds what fixtures don't (a table-less seed broke a live run that unit tests passed).
- One reviewer pass per task catches what its own tests didn't.
- Every surface, or it isn't done: CLI, Claude Code hooks and pane, fm code, MCP, other agents, Desktop, site.

## Lenses (pack: required + invented + fitted)
- Required: **inversion** (how finishing fails: stops early, calls it done when it merely stopped, loses the plan to a
  compaction or crash, plans an incomplete version, drifts off the goal, gold-plates forever); **sci-fi** (the 2030
  harness that takes one line and works for weeks to a finished result, worked back to a ledger, a verdict and a hook
  today); **self-modification** (a planner that learns from which plans held: every item added after "done" is a miss
  the next contents list prevents, measured per goal, reversible).
- Invented: **the reopened ticket** (what a user finds missing a week after done); **relay race** (a fresh session with
  zero memory resumes mid-goal exactly; the plan on disk is the only memory); **done-vs-stopped auditor** (an adversary
  that tries to prove the work merely stopped: usage limit, drive cap, no-progress stop, crash, the model saying done).
- Fitted: user value, reliability, simplicity, bold bets, blind spots.

## Gaps this Mission targets (gap map #4; planned briefs, open until the exam shows them closed)
| Gap | Tier | Brief |
|---|---|---|
| A goal ledger: contents → tasks → done-when → coverage, one record a goal lives in; epics | 4 | 1 |
| Grounded contents lists: from the user's words, the repo's surfaces and the finish standard | 3 | 2 |
| Done-vs-stopped verdict with the stop's cause | 4 | 3 |
| Clauses wired to Stop: an unmet MUST or DONE-WHEN clause blocks "done" | 3 | 4 |
| The goal carried across days, crashes and compactions | 3 | 5 |
| No held-out, child-authored exam for #4 | 3 | 6 |
| Surfaces: fm code, MCP, other agents, Desktop, site, pane, docs | 3 | 7 |

## Approaches
A. **Chosen — grow `fm mandate` into the goal ledger** (decided). The mandate is already the standing record of a
   sweeping request (text, clauses, until, a USD bound) that scout and the night run read. It gains contents items,
   each linked to its tasks and done-when, and a verdict. One standing goal per project; epics are contents items with
   several tasks. `fm goal` is the verb; `fm mandate` stays an alias.
B. A GOAL brief type whose children hang off `depends_on`. Not now: a schema change across queue, drive, archive and
   site for what one record holds.
C. A light `fm genesis` per goal (gen-0 → missions → briefs). Too heavy for an everyday goal; #13 keeps it for goals
   that rewrite Foreman itself. The ledger is what genesis's tower would read if it grows into goals.
D. Several standing goals per project. Captured: revisit when a user replaces an open goal with another while the
   first is unfinished, twice.

## Design
1. **Goal ledger — `fm goal`** (tier 4, L). `fm goal set "<goal>" [--until] [--usd]` (the mandate record grows
   `items`: `{n, text, source, done_when, tasks}`); `fm goal show` the ledger: each item → its tasks → their status and
   done-when; coverage: items with no task, open tasks captured under the goal with no item (drift); `fm goal link N
   ID`, `fm goal item "<text>" [--done-when "<check> :: <cmd>"]`. While a goal stands, `fm capture`/`fm task new`
   stamp `goal:` on the brief, and `fm goal link` places it. Ledger events `goal_set`, `goal_item`, `goal_verdict`.
2. **Grounded contents list — `fm goal plan`** (tier 3, M). Items from three sources, each tagged: the user's words
   (fmrecall.clauses, one item per clause, source `user`); the finish standard for what the repo actually ships
   (fmmission.surfaces: tests, exam scenarios, MASTER/README/CHANGELOG, a site page if user-facing, a pane line if it
   has state, each surface it belongs on; source `standard`); and a tool-less child's best-in-class list from the
   mission pack (source `model`), kept only when it names a file, symbol or surface the repo has or a user clause
   implies; the rest are shown as proposals, never items. Naming a real file is only the grounding floor, not proof
   the item matters: whether the list was right is scored by misses and by the goal exam kind (brief 6). Misses learn:
   an item added after the goal's first done claim, or a revert, re-fix or correction within 30 days of a task's close
   (fm outcomes' window), is a miss recorded by surface; `fm goal plan` adds the
   project's top misses as checklist lines and says how many past goals missed each.
3. **Done-vs-stopped verdict — `fm goal verdict`** (tier 4, M). Deterministic. **Finished** only when every item has a
   task and every task is done (a dropped one needs its logged reason), every done-when command passes on a fresh
   run now, no clause of the goal is unaccounted, and the gates are green on HEAD (fm check's same-tree reuse).
   Otherwise **stopped**, with the cause read from the ledger and the session events: usage limit, drive cap
   (DRIVE_MAX), no-progress stop, contract bound spent, waiting on the user (an open `fm ask`), paused, crash (a
   session start with no Stop after the last edit), or the model saying done with items open. Prints what's left in
   order. The verdict is Foreman's own check, so it never counts as outside proof: the goal and resume exam kinds
   (brief 6) score its false-done rate against a hidden key it never sees, and fm outcomes scores it after 30 days.
4. **Stop wired to the goal and the clauses** (tier 3, M). In `stop()`: a done claim (claims_done) while the last
   request has unaccounted clauses (fm clauses' `open`) blocks once with them; while a goal stands and its verdict is
   stopped, a done claim blocks once with the items left. Both count toward DRIVE_MAX and the no-progress stop, so
   they never trap a session. The drive, with an empty queue and an open goal item with no task, says "plan item N"
   instead of ending (full autonomy) or names it (standard).
5. **Goal across days** (tier 3, M). SessionStart and the PreCompact checkpoint carry one line: the goal, items
   done/total, the next item and its task; `fm resume` prints it; `fm run` takes the next item's task when the queue
   is empty. A goal set by a past session is re-injected every session until its verdict is finished or it is cleared.
6. **#4 exam kinds** (tier 3, M). `goal`: a tool-less child, shown only the scenario's generated module and the
   scenario format (never Foreman's code or the Missions), writes a vague goal for that module and a hidden contents
   key (4–6 items: each a test body or a README pattern), the arm gets only the goal; graded on key items met, 0
   regressions, and whether the arm's final claim matches the truth (said done with a key item unmet = a false done).
   `resume`: the same goal with half its items done and the plan on disk, the first session killed; a fresh session
   gets "continue"; graded on the remaining items met and no item redone. Child-authored, 9 per kind (3 held out),
   six languages.
7. **Surfaces** (tier 3, M). fm code (the goal line in its prompt and the same stop check), the MCP tool list (`goal`,
   read-only: ledger and verdict), the AGENTS.md block for other agents, Desktop through MCP, the site page (Goal to
   finish: items, verdicts over time, the exam line), the pane band (a goal progress line), MASTER.md, README,
   CHANGELOG.

## Exam (#4; ≥ 9 scenarios per kind, ≥ 3 held out)
| Kind | Given | Graded on |
|---|---|---|
| G-goal | a vague goal for the module, a hidden contents key (4–6 items) | key items met; 0 regressions; no false done |
| G-resume | the goal half done, the plan on disk, the first session killed; "continue" | remaining items met; none redone |
Arms: foreman (fm goal + Stop), plain ("" plugin), on the held-out third, with cost. The oracle meets every key item;
empty meets none and must never be graded done.
These kinds are the smoke tier (gen-1/seed.md rule 6): small single-defect scenarios never decide #4 on their own. The deciding end-of-run score is the long-horizon tier, on the production model: a goal replayed from Foreman's own history (the repo rolled back to the parent of a past multi-task change, that change's request as the goal, its shipped tests as the hidden checks), with a killed session and a forced compaction planted mid-run. Scored per finished goal on true-done rate, false-done claims, regressions and later reverts, interventions needed and cost per finished goal.

## Exam of the exam
1. Every key item's test passes on the oracle's render and fails on the base, in all six languages.
2. A child's key item that the base already meets is dropped and logged as an exam defect.
3. Held-out ids never appear in a train run or in tuning the contents checklist.

## Spikes (tier 4, local, throwaway)
Relay race: kill a session at five random points of a goal, a fresh one resumes from disk alone; count redone and lost
items. Reopened-ticket miner: in git history, commits within 30 days of a task's close touching its files are misses;
does `fm goal plan`'s list predict them? Done-vs-stopped adversary: craft states that make the verdict say finished
wrongly (a done-when that passes vacuously, a dropped task with no reason).

## Inbox (tier 1–2, captured)
- T-2142 goal notices only on state transitions (tier 2)
- T-2143 a byte-stable goal card so the SessionStart prefix stays cached (tier 1)
- T-2144 the goal's remaining distance as one number on the statusline and terminal title (tier 2)
- T-2145 a time-to-finish estimate from the items' history (tier 2)

## Rejected
Nothing for ambition. Only the outward halves, which need a grant the Mission can't take:
- "Publish mortality tables of how goals end": publishing leaves the machine. The local table lives in brief 3's verdict history.
- "Nudge a wrist or phone on a typed wait": outward without a grant. `fm notify` is the user's opt-in path, and T-2142 feeds it.
- "Take steers from a synced drop folder": a sync channel is outward. `fm sync` and `fm serve` already cover it under their grants.

## Tier share
Briefs: 7 (tier 4: 1 and 3; tier 3: 2, 4, 5, 6, 7), so 100% of the Mission's work is tier 3–4, plus 3 tier-4 spikes. The 4 inbox items (tier 1–2) are captured, not Mission work.

## Done when
`fm goal set/plan/show/verdict` work and are tested; a done claim with unaccounted clauses or an unfinished goal is
blocked once at Stop and never traps the session; the goal line survives a new session, a compaction and a crash; the
#4 exam runs the foreman and plain arms on its held-out third; fm code, MCP, the AGENTS.md block, the site page, the
pane line, MASTER.md, README and CHANGELOG show it.

```
FEATURE: fm goal — the mandate grows into the goal ledger: items → tasks → done-when, coverage, one standing goal
FEATURE: fm goal plan — a grounded contents list from the user's words, the repo's surfaces and the finish standard; misses learn
FEATURE: fm goal verdict — finished vs stopped, with the stop's cause, deterministic
FEATURE: Stop wiring — unaccounted clauses and an unfinished goal block a done claim once
FEATURE: goal across days — SessionStart, PreCompact, fm resume and fm run carry the goal line
FEATURE: #4 exam — G-goal and G-resume, child-authored, foreman vs plain
FEATURE: goal surfaces — fm code, MCP, AGENTS.md, site page, pane line, docs
DONE-WHEN: #4's held-out exam passes at the end-of-run exam (the production-model foreman-vs-plain and long-horizon runs
decide, gen-1/seed.md rule 6); until then the free arms and the Haiku smoke run show no regression, and no arm is graded done while
a key item is unmet
```

# Mission — Genesis as a feature (gen 1, #13)

Task: T-2093 (brief 1, fm genesis check), T-2095 (brief 2, fm genesis step), T-2099 (brief 3, fm genesis draft/spec), T-2102 (brief 4, fm genesis select/seed), T-2104 (brief 5, fm genesis drift/sweep), T-2105 (brief 6, scout offer, revert stop, /foreman:genesis skill, site verdicts), T-2112 (brief 7, fm genesis exam: #13's held-out exam, G-tower session arm), T-2113 (brief 8, charter seal + privilege diff in the sweep).

Self-contained for a fresh `fm run` in ~/.claude/foreman. Parent: gen-1/seed.md → gen-0.md §2 #13, §3.
Ideas: 606 from `fm ideas --rounds 4 --deepen 3 --falsify --crossbreed --seen` (brainstorm-20261029-233136), lenses
below; about 135 placed by tier after merging duplicates.

## Capability (gen-0 §2 #13)
`fm genesis` plus a skill: from one line, a sweeping request or nothing, it writes its own gen-0 for the project, runs
the whole tower (Seed → ≤ 8 Missions → briefs → critiques → selection → drift → sweep), writes the project's own
capability spec with a held-out exam, starts by itself when the queue runs dry or the gap map shows big gaps, and
carries over what a run learned. From gen 2 on, the feature writes the Seed.

## Lenses (pack: fitted + required + invented)
- Required: **inversion** (how Genesis fails or is abused: runs forever, rewrites rules toward easier exams, burns a
  week of usage, drifts from the user's MUSTs, grants itself something, overfits the held-out third); **sci-fi**
  (the 2030 self-writing harness, worked back to what Python and Foreman can do today); **self-modification** (Genesis
  improving its templates, exam, lenses and selection rule, each change measured, reversible and inside the NEVERs).
- Invented: **cold-start stranger** (a repo never seen, no history, one line or nothing: what the first ten minutes
  write and get wrong); **tower archaeology** (a fresh session opens a three-generation tower with no chat: what the
  files alone must say to resume); **economics of a generation** (cost and wall-clock per scenario closed; when to stop
  early, wait for a reset or spend more).
- Fitted: user value, reliability, simplicity, bold bets, blind spots.

## Gaps closed (gap map #13)
| Gap | Tier | Brief |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage grid with no empty cell; not-yet ledger retried every generation | 3 | 1 (T-2093, built) |
| Tower orchestrator: one next action from the files alone, resumable after any kill | 4 | 2 |
| gen-0 writer from one line, a sweeping request or nothing | 3 | 3 |
| Per-project capability spec with a held-out exam | 3 | 3 |
| Selection + lineage + carry-over; the feature writes the Seed | 3 | 4 |
| Drift check against gen-0 + one-shot §7 sweep | 3 | 5 |
| Auto-start from loop/scout; routing line as a core candidate | 3 | 6 |
| No exam for #13 itself | 3 | 7 |
| Nothing stops a generation from rewriting the user's MUSTs or widening its own grants | 3 | 8 |

## Approaches
A. **Chosen — the tower files are the state.** The stage is the first missing or unfinished file in a fixed order
   (gen-0 → seed → missions → their tasks closed → critiques → lineage line → drift → sweep → next seed). No journal
   to disagree with the files; a kill anywhere resumes for free; a fresh session reads the same files (archaeology).
B. A JSON state machine with a journal and schema version. Rejected for now: a second record of the same facts that
   can drift from the files; kept as the fallback if A can't express a stage (the spike in brief 2 decides).
C. A headless driver (`fm run` over the tower) that executes every step. Built on top of A later, not instead: the
   step function must exist and be tested before anything runs it unattended.
D. Make the tower a `fm loop` mode. Rejected: the loop is open-ended by design (dry yield stops it); the tower has a
   fixed shape, caps and a done test.

## Design
1. **Checker — `fm genesis check`** (built, T-2093). coverage.md: `## <area>` rows, 64 cells each
   (`- <stage> × <surface>: F|I|N/A: …`); F names an existing path, I ends with the file it builds on, N/A gives a
   reason; every gen-0 capability has its row. not-yet.md: `## <idea>` items with `- blocker:`, `- tried: a; b`
   (two different approaches), `- unblocks-with:`, and `- retried: gen-N …` or `- added: gen-N …` for the newest
   generation; `## Removed` lines say harm or duplicate. Exit 1 on any problem; `fm genesis` shows the counts.
2. **Orchestrator — `fm genesis step [--json]`** (tier 4). Prints the one next action and its command, from the files:
   no gen-0 → `fm genesis draft`; no seed → write it (gen 1: by hand from gen-0; gen ≥ 2: `fm genesis seed`); a seed
   row without its mission file → `fm mission` + `fm ideas …` for that capability; a mission whose `Task:` ids aren't
   closed → `fm focus` the first open one; no critique → write it; all critiques → `fm genesis select`; then
   `fm genesis drift`, `fm genesis sweep`, next seed. Caps: ≤ 8 seed rows, ≤ 4 levels, refuses past them. One
   `c.lock` around state changes. Each step's failure is classed retryable (rerun), user-needed (into the final
   report) or fatal (the tower stops and says why). A budget line between stages (`fmcost.quote_line`). `fm next`'s
   idle path names `fm genesis step` while a tower is open. A stalled tower (no file change in 24 h with work left)
   is named in the next session's start note. Tests: kill after every stage and resume to the same next action; a
   corrupt or out-of-shape file is refused by name; a lock collision is refused; the caps hold.
3. **gen-0 writer + spec — `fm genesis draft [LINE]`, `fm genesis spec`** (tier 3). Extraction first (project kind,
   languages, gates from CI config, the user's MUST/NEVER-shaped corrections from Foreman's memory and decisions, the
   gap map), then one tool-less model call that fills the hand gen-0's skeleton (§1–§8, MUST/NEVER/DONE-WHEN). Each
   MUST taken from the user's own words quotes its source; inferred ones are marked `(unconfirmed)`; cold-start
   assumptions are listed. Generated and vendored code is fenced out. `spec` writes spec.md: "complete and best in
   class for this kind of project" as capability rows, each with exam scenarios from `fm exam gen` in the project's
   languages (a third held out). A tiny project gets a one-generation tower; a project the exam can't run gets a spec
   with no exam, flagged. Tests: the hand gen-0's own text yields every MUST and NEVER; empty input gives a valid
   draft; a planted absurd MUST in the history is marked unconfirmed, not adopted.
4. **Selection, lineage, Seed — `fm genesis select N`, `fm genesis seed N`** (tier 3). Selection reads exam.jsonl's
   train ids only (built: gen-0 §4 keeps the held-out third out of selection): a generation's rewrite stays only if
   it closes more scenarios than its parent on the same run; a tie reverts whatever the cost (cost is reported, never
   a tie-break; both fm decide, T-2102); no reopening what the parent closed (ratchet); reruns for variance when the
   margin is one scenario on a single line. Every decision is a lineage.md line and a `fm decide`.
   The exam's held-out ids are hash-locked for the generation. `seed N` writes gen-N/seed.md from the parent seed,
   its critiques, empty coverage cells (first), not-yet items (each retried), exam scores and lineage; the Seed's
   size is capped. Tests: a child that closes fewer loses; a tie loses; a reopened scenario fails.
5. **Drift + sweep — `fm genesis drift N`, `fm genesis sweep N`** (tier 3). Drift: every unfenced MUST:/NEVER: line
   in gen-N's seed and mission files is one of gen-0's verbatim (reworded or added is drift; fenced intake blocks are
   briefs, whose MUSTs are task constraints), each file quotes gen-0's constraints or points to gen-0 (a seed points,
   never restates), and one tool-less cold read of the seed against gen-0's goal, MUSTs, NEVERs and DONE-WHEN names
   drifted lines, counted only when the seed holds them. Verdict clean, drifted or unread (no read is no pass). Sweep:
   §7's list in one command — fm genesis check, mission tasks closed or blocked with a reason, no planned/active task,
   no unreasoned block, no unmerged lane, fm docs, fm doctor, a full fm check pass on this exact tree (read, never
   rerun), an exam line for gen N, and every user-steer rule's stored `fm decide --check`, run (the steer-checks row,
   T-2167) — into gen-N/sweep.md, exit 1 on any red; a red sweep files a fix task per red row and a clean one writes
   the next seed (T-2477). step stays on either until its Verdict is
   clean. Tests: a reworded MUST, an added NEVER and an unpointed file drift; a clean seed passes; no read fails; a
   red sweep keeps step on it, a clean one moves to the next seed.
6. **Auto-start** (tier 3). When user-origin work is dry and the gap map has tier 3–4 gaps, the idle path proposes a
   blocked task "Start Genesis here?" (never a silent run), with a cooldown and a breaker on Genesis's own failure
   and revert rate; `fm pause --now` stops it. `/foreman:genesis` skill drives `fm genesis step`. The routing line in
   rules/foreman.md is protected core: a built, evaluated candidate in a worktree and `fm ask ID core` at the end.
7. **#13 exam** (tier 3). See below. A genesis arm (`fm exam run RUN --agent genesis`) runs draft + spec + one
   generation on each scenario project; the plain arm gets "make this great" with no plugin.
8. **Charter seal + privilege diff** (tier 3). `fm genesis init` records the hash of gen-0's MUST/NEVER lines; drift
   fails if a seed contradicts one; each generation lists grants and allows used (fm ask, --allow) and halts on a new
   kind it didn't have before.

## Exam (#13; ≥ 9 scenarios per kind, ≥ 3 held out)
| Kind | Given | Graded on |
|---|---|---|
| G-line | a generated project + "make this great" | draft covers every MUST, NEVER and § of the hand gen-0 checklist, and every standing-intent clause (T-2191) |
| G-none | a generated project + nothing | same checklist; the draft names what it assumed |
| G-sweep | a generated project + "super improve this" | same checklist + a tier on every brief |
| G-tower | a generated project with planted gaps (fm exam key) | one generation closes the planted gaps (found + fixed, test first) |
Each kind 9 scenarios → 6 train + 3 held out, from `fm exam gen` projects (6 languages). Arms: genesis vs plain on the
held-out third, with cost.

## Exam of the exam
1. Oracle: the hand gen-0 itself scores 100% on the checklist; an empty draft scores 0.
2. Mutation: the hand gen-0 with any one MUST or NEVER removed scores below 100% (each item is load-bearing).
3. Held-out project ids never appear in a train run; the hand checklist is never shown to the writer.

## Spikes (tier 4, local, throwaway)
Red-team twin that games the gen-0 checklist; a planted absurd MUST; a mirror-universe selector (inverted rule must
lose); a mutation-tested exam; a never-seen repo vs plain Claude (`fmbench.stranger`); rebuild-from-gen-0 challenger.

## Inbox (tier 1–2, captured)
Generation receipt and digest with a publish secret scan; a resume verdict line; statusline tower health; a time-scrub
slider on the site page; publish only on green CI; tower rewind; and the rest of the ~40 tier 1–2 titles.

## Rejected
Each with its own reason; the four that only leave the machine are parked for a grant, not killed (gen-0: anything
that leaves the machine needs its grant):
- Cross-project genome import: reads other people's Foreman state from outside this machine; parked until a grant.
- Specs sourced from competitors or dependencies: sweeping outside repos to brainstorm, which gen-0's NEVER forbids
  beyond §5's targeted form; the targeted form is fm genesis frontier.
- Earned-trust autonomy or a user proxy: Foreman would grant itself what only the user grants, which gen-0's NEVER
  forbids (grant yourself anything or lower your own guard).
- Persona bots on live products: acts on live services outside the machine; parked until a grant.
- Signed attestations: publishes signatures outside the machine; parked until a grant.
- Upstream bug reports: posts to other projects' trackers; parked until a grant (outward posting is the user's call).

## Tier share
Built here: 8 briefs, 1 at tier 4 and 7 at tier 3 (100% tier 3–4) plus 6 tier-4 spikes; tier 1–2 go to the inbox.

## Done when
`fm genesis check/step/draft/spec/select/seed/drift/sweep` work and are tested; the kill-and-resume test passes for
every stage; the #13 exam runs both arms on its held-out third and its exam-of-the-exam checks are tests; coverage.md
and not-yet.md are in the tower and `fm genesis check` exits 0; MASTER.md + CHANGELOG + the site's Genesis page show
it; the `/foreman:genesis` skill works in Claude Code; the routing candidate waits on `fm ask core`.

```
FEATURE: fm genesis check — coverage grid + not-yet ledger, exit 1 on any gap
FEATURE: fm genesis step — the tower's next action from its files alone, resumable after any kill
DONE-WHEN: killing after every stage and rerunning gives the same next action; caps and lock hold
FEATURE: fm genesis draft/spec — gen-0 from a line or nothing; per-project spec with a held-out exam
FEATURE: fm genesis select/seed — exam-gated selection into lineage.md; the feature writes the next Seed
FEATURE: fm genesis drift/sweep — gen-0 MUST/NEVER drift check, §7 sweep in one command
FEATURE: Genesis auto-start proposal + /foreman:genesis skill + routing candidate (core, fm ask)
FEATURE: #13 exam — G-line, G-none, G-sweep, G-tower kinds; genesis vs plain arms
FEATURE: charter seal + privilege diff per generation
```
